subject: math
cluster: Draw informal comparative inferences about two populations
intro: Each problem compares two random samples. Compute a center (mean) and a spread (MAD) for each sample, express the difference of the means as a multiple of the MAD using $\dfrac{|\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2|}{\text{MAD}}$, and then draw and justify an informal inference about the two populations.

items.prompt: A random sample of daily high temperatures (in $^\circ\text{F}$) from two cities is recorded. City A: $\{68, 72, 70, 74, 66\}$. City B: $\{78, 82, 80, 84, 76\}$. Both samples have the same MAD. Find each mean and the common MAD, then express the difference of the means as a multiple of the MAD and state which city is typically warmer.
items.answer: City A mean $= 70$, City B mean $= 80$, MAD $= 2.4$ for each; the means differ by $\dfrac{|80 - 70|}{2.4} \approx 4.17$ MADs, so City B is typically warmer with a large separation.

steps: Difference of means as a multiple of MAD: $\dfrac{|80 - 70|}{2.4} = \dfrac{10}{2.4} \approx 4.17$
The means differ by about $4.17$ MADs, which is a large separation, so City B is typically warmer than City A.

items.prompt: Two random samples of words are taken from a children's book and an adult novel and their lengths (in letters) recorded. Children's book: $\{3, 5, 4, 2, 6\}$. Adult novel: $\{7, 9, 8, 6, 10\}$. Find each mean and MAD, express the difference of the means as a multiple of the MAD, and infer which book typically uses longer words.
items.answer: Children's mean $= 4$, novel mean $= 8$, each MAD $= 1.2$; the means differ by $\dfrac{|8 - 4|}{1.2} \approx 3.33$ MADs, so the adult novel typically uses longer words.

steps: Difference of means as a multiple of MAD: $\dfrac{|8 - 4|}{1.2} = \dfrac{4}{1.2} \approx 3.33$
Because the random samples represent the books, we infer the adult novel typically uses longer words, with the means about $3.33$ MADs apart, a large gap.

items.prompt: A random sample of the number of pages read per day by students in two reading programs is taken. Program X: $\{20, 24, 22, 18, 26, 20\}$. Program Y: $\{30, 28, 34, 26, 30, 32\}$. Find each mean and MAD, express the difference of the means as a multiple of the MAD, and state which program's students typically read more.
items.answer: Program X mean $= 21\frac{2}{3} \approx 21.67$, Program Y mean $= 30$, $\text{MAD}_X = \dfrac{7}{3} \approx 2.33$, $\text{MAD}_Y = 2$; using the larger MAD the means differ by $\dfrac{|30 - 21.67|}{2.33} \approx 3.57$ MADs, so Program Y students typically read more.

steps: Program X deviations from $\tfrac{65}{3}$: about $1.67, 2.33, 0.33, 3.67, 4.33, 1.67$; sum $\approx 14$, so $\text{MAD}_X = \dfrac{14}{6} \approx 2.33$
Program Y deviations from $30$: $0, 2, 4, 4, 0, 2$; sum $= 12$, so $\text{MAD}_Y = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2$
Difference of means as a multiple of the spread: $\dfrac{|30 - 21.67|}{2} = \dfrac{8.33}{2} \approx 4.17$, or about $3.6$ using $\text{MAD}_X$
The means are roughly $4$ MADs apart, a large separation, so Program Y students typically read more pages per day.

items.prompt: Two random samples of plant heights (in cm) are taken from two greenhouses. Greenhouse 1: $\{12, 15, 14, 11, 13\}$. Greenhouse 2: $\{19, 22, 20, 18, 21\}$. Find each mean and MAD, express the difference of the means as a multiple of the MAD, and infer which greenhouse grows taller plants.
items.answer: Greenhouse 1 mean $= 13$, Greenhouse 2 mean $= 20$, each MAD $= 1.2$; the means differ by $\dfrac{|20 - 13|}{1.2} \approx 5.83$ MADs, so Greenhouse 2 typically grows taller plants.

steps: Difference of means as a multiple of MAD: $\dfrac{|20 - 13|}{1.2} = \dfrac{7}{1.2} \approx 5.83$
The means are nearly $6$ MADs apart, a very large separation, so Greenhouse 2 typically grows taller plants.

items.prompt: A random sample of test scores from two classes is taken. Class P: $\{82, 78, 80, 84, 76\}$. Class Q: $\{82, 70, 90, 74, 84\}$. The two samples have the same mean. Find that common mean and each MAD, then state which class is more consistent and explain why the difference-of-means-over-MAD measure is not useful here.
items.answer: Both means $= 80$; $\text{MAD}_P = 2.4$ and $\text{MAD}_Q = 6.4$, so Class P is more consistent. The difference of means is $0$, so $\dfrac{|80 - 80|}{\text{MAD}} = 0$ and tells us nothing about which is larger; the spreads are what distinguish the classes.

steps: Difference of means as a multiple of MAD: $\dfrac{|80 - 80|}{\text{MAD}} = 0$, so center alone cannot separate the classes
Since $\text{MAD}_P = 2.4 < 6.4 = \text{MAD}_Q$, Class P scores are more consistent; we must compare spread, not center, here.

items.prompt: Two random samples of commute times (in minutes) are taken on two routes. Route A: $\{25, 30, 28, 22, 35, 20\}$. Route B: $\{40, 38, 44, 42, 36, 40\}$. Find each mean and MAD, express the difference of the means as a multiple of the larger MAD, and infer which route is typically faster.
items.answer: Route A mean $= 26\frac{2}{3} \approx 26.67$, Route B mean $= 40$; $\text{MAD}_A = \dfrac{13}{3} \approx 4.33$, $\text{MAD}_B = 2$; using the larger MAD the means differ by $\dfrac{|40 - 26.67|}{4.33} \approx 3.08$ MADs, so Route A is typically faster (shorter commute).

steps: Route A deviations from $\tfrac{80}{3}$: about $1.67, 3.33, 1.33, 4.67, 8.33, 6.67$; sum $\approx 26$, so $\text{MAD}_A = \dfrac{26}{6} \approx 4.33$
Route B deviations from $40$: $0, 2, 4, 2, 4, 0$; sum $= 12$, so $\text{MAD}_B = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2$
Difference of means using the larger MAD: $\dfrac{|40 - 26.67|}{4.33} = \dfrac{13.33}{4.33} \approx 3.1$
The means are about $3$ MADs apart, a large separation, so Route A typically has the shorter commute and is faster.

items.prompt: A random sample of the number of free throws made (out of 10) by players on two teams is taken. Team Red: $\{6, 7, 5, 8, 4\}$. Team Blue: $\{6, 6, 7, 5, 6\}$. The teams have the same mean. Find the common mean and each MAD, and state which team is more reliable at free throws and why.
items.answer: Both means $= 6$; $\text{MAD}_{\text{Red}} = 1.2$ and $\text{MAD}_{\text{Blue}} = 0.4$, so Team Blue is more reliable (smaller spread) even though both make the same number on average.

steps: The means are equal, so $\dfrac{|6 - 6|}{\text{MAD}} = 0$ and center does not distinguish the teams
Since $\text{MAD}_{\text{Blue}} = 0.4 < 1.2 = \text{MAD}_{\text{Red}}$, Team Blue is more consistent and therefore more reliable at free throws.

items.prompt: Two random samples of weekly allowances (in dollars) are taken from two neighborhoods. Neighborhood M: $\{10, 12, 8, 14, 6\}$. Neighborhood N: $\{15, 17, 13, 19, 11\}$. Find each mean and MAD, express the difference of the means as a multiple of the MAD, and infer which neighborhood typically gives higher allowances.
items.answer: Neighborhood M mean $= \$10$, Neighborhood N mean $= \$15$, each MAD $= 2.4$; the means differ by $\dfrac{|15 - 10|}{2.4} \approx 2.08$ MADs, so Neighborhood N typically gives higher allowances.

steps: Difference of means as a multiple of MAD: $\dfrac{|15 - 10|}{2.4} = \dfrac{5}{2.4} \approx 2.08$
The means are about $2$ MADs apart, a moderate separation, so Neighborhood N typically gives higher allowances.

items.prompt: A random sample of the number of hours of sleep per night is taken from two groups. Teens: $\{7, 9, 6, 8, 5\}$. Adults: $\{7, 8, 6, 7, 7\}$. Find each mean and MAD, express the difference of the means as a multiple of the larger MAD, and decide whether the difference in typical sleep is large or small relative to the spread.
items.answer: Teens mean $= 7$, Adults mean $= 7$; $\text{MAD}_{\text{Teens}} = 1.2$, $\text{MAD}_{\text{Adults}} = 0.4$. The means are equal so the difference is $0$ MADs; the groups differ only in spread, with teens' sleep more variable.

steps: Difference of means as a multiple of MAD: $\dfrac{|7 - 7|}{1.2} = 0$, so typical sleep is the same
The groups are distinguished only by spread: teens' sleep is more variable ($1.2$ vs $0.4$), while the typical amount is identical.

items.prompt: Two random samples of fish lengths (in cm) are taken from two lakes. Lake East: $\{14, 16, 12, 18, 20\}$. Lake West: $\{24, 26, 22, 28, 30\}$. Find each mean and MAD, express the difference of the means as a multiple of the MAD, and infer which lake typically has longer fish.
items.answer: Lake East mean $= 16$, Lake West mean $= 26$, each MAD $= 2.4$; the means differ by $\dfrac{|26 - 16|}{2.4} \approx 4.17$ MADs, so Lake West typically has longer fish.

steps: Difference of means as a multiple of MAD: $\dfrac{|26 - 16|}{2.4} = \dfrac{10}{2.4} \approx 4.17$
The means are about $4.17$ MADs apart, a large separation, so Lake West typically has longer fish.

items.prompt: A random sample of the number of customers per hour is taken at two cafes. Cafe One: $\{18, 22, 20, 16, 24\}$. Cafe Two: $\{21, 19, 20, 22, 18\}$. Find each mean and MAD, express the difference of the means as a multiple of the larger MAD, and decide whether the cafes differ meaningfully in typical traffic.
items.answer: Cafe One mean $= 20$, Cafe Two mean $= 20$; $\text{MAD}_{\text{One}} = 2.4$, $\text{MAD}_{\text{Two}} = 1.2$. The means are equal, so the difference is $0$ MADs; typical traffic is the same, but Cafe One's traffic is more variable.

steps: Difference of means as a multiple of MAD: $\dfrac{|20 - 20|}{2.4} = 0$
Typical traffic is the same for both cafes, but Cafe One is more variable ($2.4$ vs $1.2$), so they differ in consistency, not in center.

items.prompt: Two random samples of jump distances (in inches) are taken from two age groups at a track meet. Group 9: $\{40, 44, 42, 38, 46\}$. Group 11: $\{52, 56, 54, 50, 58\}$. Find each mean and MAD, express the difference of the means as a multiple of the MAD, and infer which group typically jumps farther.
items.answer: Group 9 mean $= 42$, Group 11 mean $= 54$, each MAD $= 2.4$; the means differ by $\dfrac{|54 - 42|}{2.4} = 5$ MADs, so Group 11 typically jumps farther.

steps: Difference of means as a multiple of MAD: $\dfrac{|54 - 42|}{2.4} = \dfrac{12}{2.4} = 5$
The means are exactly $5$ MADs apart, a very large separation, so Group 11 typically jumps farther.

items.prompt: A random sample of battery life (in hours) is taken for two phone models. Model S: $\{10, 12, 11, 9, 13\}$. Model T: $\{11, 13, 12, 10, 14\}$. Find each mean and MAD, express the difference of the means as a multiple of the MAD, and decide whether the difference in typical battery life is large or small relative to the spread.
items.answer: Model S mean $= 11$, Model T mean $= 12$, each MAD $= 1.2$; the means differ by $\dfrac{|12 - 11|}{1.2} \approx 0.83$ MADs, a small separation, so the typical battery lives are close relative to the spread.

steps: Model S deviations from $11$: $1, 1, 0, 2, 2$, so MAD $= \dfrac{6}{5} = 1.2$
Model T deviations from $12$: $1, 1, 0, 2, 2$, so MAD $= \dfrac{6}{5} = 1.2$
Difference of means as a multiple of MAD: $\dfrac{|12 - 11|}{1.2} = \dfrac{1}{1.2} \approx 0.83$
The means are less than $1$ MAD apart, a small separation, so Model T is only slightly better on average and the difference is minor relative to the spread.

items.prompt: Two random samples of seedling growth (in mm) after one week are taken under two light conditions. Low light: $\{6, 8, 7, 5, 9, 7\}$. High light: $\{14, 12, 16, 13, 11, 15\}$. Find each mean and MAD, express the difference of the means as a multiple of the larger MAD, and infer which light condition produces more growth.
items.answer: Low light mean $= 7$, High light mean $= 13.5$; $\text{MAD}_{\text{Low}} = 1$, $\text{MAD}_{\text{High}} \approx 1.5$; using the larger MAD the means differ by $\dfrac{|13.5 - 7|}{1.5} \approx 4.33$ MADs, so high light produces more growth.

steps: Low light deviations from $7$: $1, 1, 0, 2, 2, 0$; sum $= 6$, so $\text{MAD}_{\text{Low}} = \dfrac{6}{6} = 1$
High light deviations from $13.5$: $0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 0.5, 2.5, 1.5$; sum $= 9$, so $\text{MAD}_{\text{High}} = \dfrac{9}{6} = 1.5$
Difference of means using the larger MAD: $\dfrac{|13.5 - 7|}{1.5} = \dfrac{6.5}{1.5} \approx 4.33$
The means are about $4.33$ MADs apart, a large separation, so the high light condition typically produces more seedling growth.

items.prompt: A random sample of points scored per game is taken for two basketball players. Player Ava: $\{16, 20, 18, 14, 22\}$. Player Ben: $\{19, 18, 17, 18, 18\}$. Find each mean and MAD, express the difference of the means as a multiple of the larger MAD, then give a full comparative inference: who typically scores more, who is more consistent, and which player you would rely on for a steady contribution.
items.answer: Ava mean $= 18$, Ben mean $= 18$; $\text{MAD}_{\text{Ava}} = 2.4$, $\text{MAD}_{\text{Ben}} = 0.4$. The means are equal, so the difference is $0$ MADs and neither typically scores more. Ben is far more consistent ($0.4$ vs $2.4$), so you would rely on Ben for a steady contribution.

steps: Difference of means as a multiple of MAD: $\dfrac{|18 - 18|}{2.4} = 0$, so neither typically scores more
Comparing spread, $\text{MAD}_{\text{Ben}} = 0.4 < 2.4 = \text{MAD}_{\text{Ava}}$, so Ben is much more consistent; for a steady, dependable contribution you would rely on Ben.
